Prolonged overcast conditions or unexpected PV system failures can result in periods when backup from the power grid or energy storage assets is needed to meet electricity demand. While these challenges can typically be managed during peacetime through careful planning and reserves, the situation becomes more critical in a contested or wartime scenario. In such environments, the unpredictability of energy generation could be exacerbated by disruptions to supply chains, cyberattacks, or intentional damage to infrastructure. Naturally inconsistent and unpredictable wind patterns make wind energy especially uncertain (Saxena et al. 2024), complicating fixed generation planning and raising concerns about system reliability (Saxena et al. 2024). 2.5 Distributed Nature of Advanced Energy Assets The increasing role of DERs, such as those operated by private solar power plant owners and other nontraditional power producers, makes grid management more challenging (Rickerson, 5 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Gillis, and Bulkeley 2024). Although DERs can enhance the resilience of defense-critical infrastructure by decentralizing power generation, the proliferation of non-utility-owned devices (including by homeowners) has made electric sector reliability increasingly dependent on assets sourced from companies with links to potentially hostile foreign entities. Moreover, the growing number of interconnected devices (and the increasing presence of digital, often unregulated connections) introduces new vectors for cyber intrusion, especially when those connections are poorly secured or lack consistent oversight. The energy sector is accelerating the convergence of OT and information technology (IT), allowing adversaries to apply well-established IT attack strategies to infiltrate protected OT networks. Cyberattacks could degrade power quality and provision to DOW installations, disrupting mission readiness and forcing reliance on limited- duration backup systems. Beyond direct military bases, such attacks could also target the Defense Industrial Base, cutting off power to critical nodes, such as munitions plants, aircraft manufacturers, and key petroleum-based fuel pipelines. Interruptions to these assets would not only slow production and resupply but could cascade across logistics and sustainment operations, undermining the broader defense posture. DOW advocacy for cybersecurity minimums for local grid providers could improve resistance to cyberattacks. DERs are often connected through inverters. If these devices are not properly managed or controlled, they can create issues with power factor correction, harmonics, and phase imbalances. These factors could degrade the quality of the power supplied to defense infrastructure and could require sophisticated grid management solutions to maintain reliability. DER integration into the grid requires more advanced management systems to efficiently balance supply and demand (Horowitz et al. 2019), but many utility providers are not yet fully equipped to integrate DERs in a way that optimally supports critical national security and defense missions, particularly during emergencies when grid stability is most crucial. The rapid proliferation of DERs can outpace planned grid reinforcement, creating a trade-off between enabling local energy resilience and the technical strain on underprepared utility infrastructure.
